isolate.title: Look at the busiest value first
isolate.concept: Start with the most likely place, and check it before trusting it. A filter pill keeps one value, and is easy to undo.
isolate.narration: Start with the most likely place. Filter ${var.field} to the value with the most requests: in its Top values, click the + next to it. (Add filter works too.)
isolate.reasoning: The busiest value is the most likely place for the errors, but not a certain one. Filtering to it lets you check.
isolate.evidence: A filter pill keeps only the busiest value's requests.

demonstration.narration: I'll start where the errors are most likely: I'll filter ${var.field} to the value with the most requests.
demonstration.reasoning: The busiest value is the most likely place, not a certain one. A filter pill keeps only its requests so we can check them, and the pill is easy to undo.
demonstration.evidence: The ${var.field}: ${param.incident.decoy} filter pill, the small box under the query bar, keeps only those requests. Next, we check whether they are failing.

demonstration.narration: I'll open one failed request to check its ${var.field}, status code and error together.
demonstration.reasoning: A total can look convincing even when it includes other records. Opening one typical event shows the key values together, which a count alone can't do.
demonstration.evidence: This failed request has ${param.incident.finding}, status ${param.incident.status} and ${param.incident.error_type} together. ${truth.conclusion}

goal.title: See where most requests go
goal.concept: A field's Top values count every request in the window. The value with the most traffic is the most likely place for a problem, so it's a good place to look first. It isn't proof.
goal.narration: The report doesn't say which endpoint or service is failing. Open the ${var.field} field in the sidebar and read its Top values. Which value has the most requests? That's the most likely place to look first.
goal.reasoning: Filtering on a guessed endpoint would assume the answer. The Top values show where most of the window's traffic really goes, which is the most likely place for errors.
goal.evidence: The field's Top values show one value with far more of the window's requests than any other.

demonstration.narration: The report doesn't say which endpoint or service is failing. I'll check ${var.field} Top values to see where most of this window's requests go.
demonstration.reasoning: Filtering on a guessed endpoint would assume the answer. Top values count every request in the window, so where we look first comes from the data.
demonstration.evidence: The highlighted row, ${param.incident.decoy}, has the most requests in the window, ahead of every other ${var.field} value. With the most traffic, it's the most likely place for the errors, so we'll look there first. Busy doesn't prove it's failing, though.

goal.title: Check whether those requests are failing
goal.concept: The most likely place still has to be checked. A status code's Top values show at a glance whether requests succeeded or failed.
goal.narration: Is this where the errors are? Open the http.response.status_code field and read its Top values for these requests.
goal.reasoning: Busy isn't the same as failing. The status codes show whether this traffic has the server errors from the report.
goal.evidence: The status code Top values show whether these requests are failing.

demonstration.narration: Busy isn't the same as failing. I'll check http.response.status_code Top values for these requests.
demonstration.reasoning: The busiest value was only the most likely place. Its status codes show whether it really has the server errors from the report.
demonstration.evidence: Every ${param.incident.decoy} request returned 200, with no server errors at all. The busiest value is healthy, so the errors must be somewhere else. Next, we'll look at everything except it.

hints: Check whether the busiest value's requests are actually failing.
Open the http.response.status_code field in the sidebar and read its Top values (or add it as a column).

drifts.note: You opened ${action.field}. This step checks whether these requests are failing, so read their status codes.

goal.title: Look past the busiest value
goal.concept: A filter pill can include its value or exclude it. Turning it around shows everything except that value.
goal.narration: The busiest value is healthy, so look everywhere else. Click the ${var.field} pill and choose Exclude results. The same filter then leaves that value out.
goal.reasoning: Leaving out the healthy traffic you've already checked keeps everything else in view, without building a new filter.
goal.evidence: The pill now reads NOT, so everything except the busiest value is in view.

demonstration.narration: The busiest value is healthy, so I'll turn its pill around to look at everything else.
demonstration.reasoning: A filter pill can include its value or exclude it. Turning this one around leaves out the healthy traffic we've already checked, with no new filter to build.
demonstration.evidence: The pill now reads NOT ${var.field}: ${param.incident.decoy}. The requests we checked are left out, and the rest of the window is back in view.

hints: Look at everything except the busiest value, using the filter you already have.

Turn the ${param.incident.decoy} pill to Exclude results; Show me can do it for you.

goal.title: Keep only the server errors
goal.concept: A range query matches every value between two limits. So one query catches every 5xx status code, whatever the exact code.
goal.narration: Now keep only the server errors. In the query bar, use a range on http.response.status_code that takes every code from 500 up.
goal.reasoning: HTTP 5xx codes are server errors, and a release can produce any of them. A range catches them all, where a filter for one code would miss the rest.
goal.evidence: Only server errors remain, so you can see where the failures are.

demonstration.narration: Now I'll keep only the server errors, with a range query on the status code.
demonstration.reasoning: HTTP 5xx codes are server errors, and a release can produce any of them. http.response.status_code >= 500 catches every one, where a filter for a single code would miss the rest.
demonstration.evidence: Every request left is a server error, and the histogram shows when they began. Next, we'll see where they are.

hints: Keep every server error, whatever its exact code, and nothing that succeeded.
KQL compares numbers with >, >=, < and <=. In the query bar, a range on http.response.status_code from 500 up keeps every 5xx code. (Add filter with ‘is between’ 500 and 599 works too.)
Type http.response.status_code >= 500; Show me can do it for you.

goal.title: See where the server errors are
goal.concept: Inside the failures, a field's Top values show where they happen.
goal.narration: Only server errors are left. Open ${var.field}'s Top values again. Which value do the errors share?
goal.reasoning: The first look showed where most traffic goes. The same field, read inside the failures, shows where the errors are.
goal.evidence: The ${var.field} Top values show the value the server errors share.

demonstration.narration: Now that only server errors are in view, I'll check ${var.field} Top values again.
demonstration.reasoning: The first look showed where most traffic goes. The same field, read inside the failures, shows where the errors are.
demonstration.evidence: Every server error left is on ${param.incident.finding}, which has less traffic than ${param.incident.decoy}. The busiest value was never where the errors were. Opening one will show which error they carry.
